templates.title: Short clicks and long clicks on search results
templates.subtopic: LEAD over a user's event stream, dwell thresholds, page-level flags

sections.scenario: A web search product logs, for every results page it serves, the page itself and what the searcher did on it: clicks on results and returns to the page with the back button. A click followed by a quick return (a short click) suggests the result did not satisfy; a click the searcher stays away from (a long click) suggests it did. The search-quality team wants, per query, the share of results pages that earned at least one long click, worst queries first.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns query, pages, clicks, short_clicks, long_click_pages, long_click_rate, ordered by long_click_rate, query, for every query with at least {{min_pages}} results pages. A user's events are all the page_events of that user's pages, in event_ts, event_id order. The dwell of a click is the time from the click to the same user's next event, whatever page it is on. A click is long if its dwell is at least {{long_s}} seconds, or if the user has no later event at all; otherwise it is short. pages counts the query's results pages, clicks and short_clicks count their clicks, long_click_pages counts pages with at least one long click, and long_click_rate = long_click_pages / pages rounded to 4 decimal places. {{next_rule}} {{dup_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). The threshold is inclusive: a dwell of exactly {{long_s}} seconds is long. Pages with no clicks count in pages. The sample has {{pages}} pages and {{events}} events.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, traffic and threshold. user_id is a pseudonymous browser identifier. Real dwell measurement has more signals (tabs, app switches); this exercise uses only the logged events.
sections.criteria: Dwell from the user's next event across pages, in a deterministic order; inclusive threshold; a click with no later event is long; pages without clicks kept; page-level "has a long click"; duplicate clicks removed before LEAD (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss threshold choice, tabs and small-sample noise.

clarifications.q: What ends a click's dwell?
clarifications.a: The same user's next event of any kind: a return, another click, or the serve of a new results page.

clarifications.q: The click is the user's last event.
clarifications.a: The user never came back: it is a long click.

clarifications.q: Is a dwell of exactly {{long_s}} seconds long?
clarifications.a: Yes. At least {{long_s}} seconds is long.

clarifications.q: A page has two long clicks.
clarifications.a: It counts once in long_click_pages; both clicks count in clicks.

clarifications.q: How is the rate rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of long_click_pages / pages, half away from zero.

hints: Join page_events to results_pages to get the user, then LEAD(event_ts) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY event_ts, event_id). Partitioning by page would miss a new search.
Classify clicks after the window function; keep every page (a LEFT JOIN from results_pages) so pages without clicks stay in the denominator.
Aggregate to the page first (BOOL_OR for "has a long click"), then to the query.
followups: The threshold of {{long_s}} seconds is arbitrary. How would you choose it from data, and how would you report sensitivity to it?
Users open results in new tabs, so the next event may come from another tab while they are still reading. What does that do to dwell, and what extra logging would you ask for?
A long-click rate per query is noisy for rare queries. How would you rank the "worst" queries without the list being all one-page queries?
At billions of searches a day, how would you compute this daily when a user's next event can land after midnight or arrive late from a phone?

rules.ask: If you partition LEAD by page, what dwell does a click get when the user's next action is a brand-new search?
What happens to a results page where nobody clicked anything?
Why does this report count pages with a long click rather than average the dwell of clicks?
What does your query do with a click that has no later event, and why is long the right answer here?
If a click is logged twice, what dwell does the first copy get, and how does that bias the report?

templates.title: Audience retention curve from played ranges
templates.subtopic: interval stabbing on a generated grid, merging overlapping intervals

sections.scenario: A video platform shows creators an audience-retention curve: for each moment of a video, the share of views that were still watching at that moment. The player reports which parts of the video each view actually played, as ranges of video position in seconds. You are writing the query behind the curve, sampled at checkpoints every {{step}}% of each video's length.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns video_id, pct, viewers, retention: one row for every video in videos and every checkpoint pct = 0, {{step}}, …, {{last_pct}}, ordered by video_id, pct. A checkpoint's position is floor(duration_s * pct / 100) seconds. A played range covers positions start_s ≤ position < end_s (half-open). viewers is the number of counted views of the video with at least one range covering the checkpoint's position; retention = viewers / counted views of the video, rounded to 4 decimal places. {{range_rule}} {{play_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). Checkpoints nobody reached appear with 0 viewers and retention 0. A range is clipped to [0, duration_s) before anything else. The sample has {{views}} views and {{ranges}} ranges.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical videos and viewing behaviour, at one-second resolution. Real retention reports handle ads, playback speed and live streams; this exercise does not.
sections.criteria: A complete video × checkpoint grid with integer positions; half-open coverage; distinct views per checkpoint; zero rows kept; ranges clipped to the video; engaged-view filter from merged (not summed) ranges applied to numerator and denominator alike (Very Hard); correct rounding and order; can discuss the boundary-event formulation at scale.

clarifications.q: Does a range ending exactly at a checkpoint's position cover it?
clarifications.a: No. Ranges are half-open; one starting exactly there does.

clarifications.q: A view rewinds and plays the checkpoint twice.
clarifications.a: It counts once.

clarifications.q: Which checkpoints exist?
clarifications.a: 0, {{step}}, … up to {{last_pct}}: every multiple of {{step}} below 100.

clarifications.q: What is the position for 30% of a 125-second video?
clarifications.a: floor(125 × 30 / 100) = 37 seconds.

clarifications.q: How is retention rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of viewers over counted views, half away from zero.

hints: Build the grid first: videos × generate_series(0, 99, {{step}}), with the position computed in integers.
Join ranges to the grid on start_s <= pos AND pos < end_s, then COUNT(DISTINCT view_id); LEFT JOIN that back onto the grid for the zero rows.
Distinct seconds played per view: merge overlapping ranges (a running MAX(end_s) over the previous rows starts a new island when start_s is past it), then sum the island lengths.
followups: The curve is shown per second for a two-hour video with 10 million views. Why is the grid join expensive, and how would you compute it with +1/−1 events at range boundaries and a running sum instead?
Creators compare the curve with "typical" videos of similar length. What would you precompute so that comparison is cheap and fair?
Played ranges arrive in batches from the player, possibly hours late and possibly twice. How would you keep the curve correct and idempotent?
A view at 2× speed covers twice the video per second of wall time. Does it change this report? Which other report would it change?

rules.ask: A range ends exactly at a checkpoint's position. Does your condition count it, and should it?
A viewer rewinds across a checkpoint. How many times does your query count them there?
How big is your grid for per-second checkpoints over every video, and what would you do instead?
Two ranges of one view overlap. How many seconds does your played-time calculation give, and how many distinct seconds were watched?
Where does a checkpoint that nobody reached go in your result?

templates.title: Impression share and why it was lost, from auction logs
templates.subtopic: per-group ranking with ROW_NUMBER, top-1 per entity, conditional aggregation

sections.scenario: A search advertising platform tells advertisers their impression share: of the auctions their campaign was eligible for, the share in which an ad was shown, and how the rest were lost, to budget or to rank. You have one auction log and one bid log, and a deliberately simplified auction model (stated below, hypothetical) to reproduce the report from them.
sections.problem: Write one PostgreSQL query that returns auction_date, campaign_id, eligible, impressions, top_impressions, impression_share, lost_budget_share, lost_rank_share: one row per UTC date of auction_ts and campaign with at least one eligible auction, ordered by auction_date, campaign_id. A campaign is eligible for every auction in which it has a bid. In each auction: a campaign with budget_limited = true does not enter and is lost to budget; the other campaigns are ranked by ad_rank descending, and the first slots of them are shown at positions 1, 2, …; every other entered campaign is lost to rank. top_impressions counts auctions shown at position 1. The three shares are impressions, lost-to-budget and lost-to-rank auctions divided by eligible, each rounded to 4 decimal places. {{min_rule}} {{ads_rule}}
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). A budget-limited campaign never takes a position, so it can never push another campaign out of a slot. The sample has {{auctions}} auctions and {{bids}} bid rows.
sections.assumptions: The auction model, ranks, slots and thresholds are hypothetical and much simpler than any real ad auction; they exist to make the report computable. Pricing is out of scope.
sections.criteria: Budget-limited campaigns excluded before ranking; a deterministic ranking within each auction; slots respected; the minimum rank inclusive and ties broken by campaign_id (Hard+); one entrant per campaign with its best ad and eligibility counted once (Very Hard); shares over eligible auctions with correct rounding; UTC dates; deterministic order; can discuss time zones, estimated eligibility and scale.

clarifications.q: Does a budget-limited campaign still use up a position?
clarifications.a: No. It does not enter, so the next campaign moves up.

clarifications.q: Which date does an auction belong to?
clarifications.a: The UTC date of auction_ts.

clarifications.q: Do the three shares always add up to 1?
clarifications.a: Before rounding, yes: every eligible auction is shown, lost to budget or lost to rank. After rounding to 4 places they may differ by a tiny amount.

clarifications.q: What if a campaign has no bid in an auction?
clarifications.a: It was not eligible; that auction is not in its denominator at all.

clarifications.q: How are shares rounded?
clarifications.a: ROUND(…, 4) of each count over eligible, half away from zero.

hints: Reduce the bids to one row per (auction, campaign) first, even if the sample looks like it already is.
Rank only the entered campaigns: filter, then ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY auction_id ORDER BY ad_rank DESC, campaign_id), and LEFT JOIN the positions back onto every eligible pair.
One row per (auction, campaign) with three booleans (shown, lost to budget, lost to rank) makes the final aggregation a set of COUNT(*) FILTER (…)s.
followups: Advertisers want impression share by hour of day in their own time zone. What changes, and which auctions move to a different day?
"Eligible" here is any auction with a bid. In a real system eligibility is itself estimated (targeting, quality thresholds). How would you report an estimated denominator honestly?
At billions of auctions a day, how would you partition the bid log, and can you compute the ranking without a shuffle by campaign?
Budget-limited auctions cluster late in the day. How would you use this report to tell an advertiser how much more traffic a larger budget would buy?

rules.ask: Two campaigns tie on ad_rank. What positions does RANK give them, and can that show more ads than there are slots?
Where in your query does a budget-limited campaign stop taking a position from someone else?
Your ROW_NUMBER partitions by auction. What is in the ORDER BY, and is it deterministic?
Is a campaign's daily impression share the average of its per-auction outcomes, or the ratio of the totals? Is there a difference here?
A campaign has three ads in one auction. How many times is it eligible, and how many slots can it take?

templates.title: Trending queries per window with a lateness bound
templates.subtopic: event-time windows, watermarks, heaps and top-K

sections.scenario: A search product's trends panel shows the top queries in each window of event time. Searches reach the aggregator out of order, some by minutes: a phone may have been offline. The aggregator waits a bounded time for stragglers, then publishes the window and drops anything that arrives for it later, counting what it dropped.
sections.problem: Implement trending(events, width, lateness, k, distinct_users=False). events is a list of (event_ts, user_id, query) in arrival order, with event_ts ≥ 0 in seconds. An event belongs to the window starting at event_ts - event_ts % width. The watermark is the largest event_ts among the events that have arrived so far, minus lateness; before the first event there is none. Process events in order: an event whose window end (start + width) is less than or equal to the watermark of the events before it is dropped; otherwise it is accepted into its window, then the watermark is updated, and every window whose end is at or below the new watermark closes. At the end of input every remaining window closes. Return (windows, dropped): windows lists (window_start, top) for every window that accepted at least one event, in ascending window_start; top holds up to k (query, count) pairs. {{count_rule}} {{tie_rule}} dropped is the number of dropped events.
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 events; width ≥ 1, lateness ≥ 0, k ≥ 1. Thousands of windows can be open at once when lateness is large: per-event work must not grow with the number of open windows.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical traffic and query texts. Event times are trusted (no clock skew correction). The output is the published panel, so a window, once closed, never changes.
sections.criteria: Correct event-time windows; watermark from the maximum event time, never moving back; drop rule at the exact boundary; late events opening new windows; windows closed through a heap rather than a scan; deterministic top-k with the tie-break; distinct users when required; a clear complexity argument; credible discussion of heavy hitters and multi-partition watermarks.

clarifications.q: Does a window close when the watermark equals its end?
clarifications.a: Yes. A window [s, s + width) closes as soon as the watermark reaches s + width, and an event for it after that is dropped.

clarifications.q: Does an old event move the watermark back?
clarifications.a: No. The watermark only ever advances: it uses the largest event_ts seen so far.

clarifications.q: Can a late event open a window that has no events yet?
clarifications.a: Yes, if that window has not closed (its end is still above the watermark).

clarifications.q: Is the dropped event itself used to advance the watermark?
clarifications.a: Its event_ts is older than the watermark's source, so it cannot advance it either way.

clarifications.q: What if the input is empty?
clarifications.a: Return ([], 0).

hints: Keep a dict from window start to a counter (or a dict of user sets), and a min-heap of open window starts.
Only an event that raises the maximum event time can close windows; then pop from the heap while the smallest start's window end is at or below the watermark.
For the top k of a closing window, heapq.nsmallest(k, items, key=lambda qc: (-qc[1], qc[0])) is O(d log k) for d distinct queries.
followups: The panel must show a provisional top 10 for the open window, updated on every event. How do you maintain it without re-sorting the window's counts each time?
A window has 50 million distinct queries. Replace the exact counter with a bounded-memory heavy-hitters structure (Misra–Gries or Count-Min with a heap). What error guarantee do you give the panel?
Events come from 2 000 partitions with their own watermarks. How do you combine them, and what does one idle partition do to every window?
Product wants to re-open a window when a large batch of late data arrives. What does that do to consumers of the published panel, and how would you version the output instead?

rules.ask: How many open windows does your loop visit per event when lateness is 2 500 windows long?
Can the same window start be pushed onto your heap twice? What happens if it is?
The rule is defined on event time. What would a processing-time window publish for a phone that was offline for ten minutes?
Counter.most_common(k) breaks ties by insertion order. Does that satisfy the tie-break this panel needs?
Distinct users per query per window needs a set per pair. How would you bound that memory with a sketch, and what does it cost in accuracy?

templates.title: Autocomplete suggestions from a sharded query log
templates.subtopic: prefix indexes, top-k per key, text normalisation

sections.scenario: A search box suggests completions as people type. A nightly job builds the suggestion table from the day's query log, which is written by many servers: the same query appears in several shards, each with its own count. Policy removes some words from suggestions entirely. You are writing the function that turns the log into the suggestions for a batch of typed prefixes.
sections.problem: Implement suggest(entries, prefixes, k, blocked=None). entries is a list of (query_text, searches); a query's total is the sum of searches over all its rows. {{text_rule}} {{blocked_rule}} For each string in prefixes, in order, return up to k suggestions: the queries that start with that prefix (str.startswith; the empty prefix matches every query), ordered by total searches descending, then alphabetically. Return a list with one list per prefix; a prefix nothing starts with gets [].
sections.constraints: Up to 200 000 log rows, about 100 000 distinct queries, and 50 000 prefixes of up to 8 characters; k ≤ 10. Checking every query for every prefix is far too slow.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical log, counts and blocked words. Real suggestion systems also weigh freshness, location and personal history; this exercise uses only counts.
sections.criteria: Sums across shards after normalising; correct ordering with the tie-break; empty and trailing-space prefixes handled; whole-word blocking (Very Hard); one ranked pass or an index rather than a scan per prefix; a clear complexity argument; credible discussion of freshness, trie memory and the distinct-user privacy floor.

clarifications.q: Is a query equal to the prefix a valid suggestion?
clarifications.a: Yes. startswith is true for it.

clarifications.q: Two queries have the same total.
clarifications.a: Alphabetical order (Python string comparison) breaks the tie.

clarifications.q: Can the same prefix appear twice in prefixes?
clarifications.a: Yes. Answer it each time.

clarifications.q: Do I sum counts before or after normalising?
clarifications.a: Normalise first; variants of one query are one query.

clarifications.q: What should a prefix that matches nothing return?
clarifications.a: An empty list.

hints: Sum into a dict keyed by the normalised text first; everything after works on distinct queries.
Sort the distinct queries once by (-total, query). Walking that order, each prefix's suggestions are simply the first k queries you meet that start with it.
Only the prefixes that were asked for need a list, and only their lengths are worth slicing: for each query, try q[:n] for each requested length n.
followups: Suggestions must update every few minutes as news breaks. How do you combine yesterday's table with a stream of fresh counts without rebuilding it?
A trie with the top k stored at every node answers in O(length). What does it cost in memory for 100 million queries, and how would you shard it?

The privacy policy says a query may be suggested only if many distinct users searched it. How do you enforce that when counts come from shards, and why can't you add distinct-user counts across shards?
Users make typos. How would you still suggest "weather" to someone who typed "waeth", and what does that cost per keystroke?

rules.ask: How many startswith checks does your solution make for 50 000 prefixes over 100 000 queries?
What do you store at each trie node, and how much memory is that for 100 000 queries with k = 10?
Your range for a one-letter prefix holds thousands of queries. What does picking the top k from it cost per prefix, and how would you avoid paying it again for the same prefix?
Which key gives you count descending and text ascending in one heap, and why does the tie-break matter here?
Blocking "dough" must keep "doughnut shop". How does your check avoid matching inside a word?

templates.title: Earliest arrival over time-dependent road segments
templates.subtopic: time-dependent shortest paths, waiting at junctions, closures

sections.scenario: A maps product estimates arrival times from typical traffic. Historical speeds give every road segment a travel-time profile: the time it takes depends on when you enter it, in fixed time-of-day buckets. A delivery-planning feature lets a driver wait at a junction (a loading bay, a car park) whenever waiting gets them to the destination sooner, for example when a jam ahead is about to clear. You are writing the routine that answers "what is the earliest I can be there?" over one snapshot of profiles.
sections.problem: Implement earliest_arrival(segments, source, target, depart, bucket_min). Each segment is (from_junction, to_junction, profile) and is one-way. Times are whole minutes from the start of the day. A car that enters a segment at minute t uses bucket j = min(t // bucket_min, len(profile) - 1) (the last bucket applies for ever once the profile ends) and reaches the far junction at minute t + profile[j]. You are at source at minute depart and may wait any whole number of minutes at any junction, but not on a segment. Return the earliest minute at which you can be at target, or None if no sequence of segments reaches it. If source == target, return depart. {{traffic_rule}} {{bucket_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 60 000 junctions and 180 000 segments; every profile in one call has the same number of buckets (at most 24); travel times are whole minutes ≥ 1. Expect roughly O(E log V) work with a small factor for scanning buckets. Simulating the network minute by minute, or relaxing every segment until nothing changes, is too slow at this size.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical road graphs and profiles. The travel time is fixed by the minute you enter a segment; it does not change while you are on it. Real routing systems also model turn costs, live incidents and uncertainty; this exercise does not.
sections.criteria: Correct bucket arithmetic at boundaries and after the last bucket; waiting handled by considering the first minute of each later bucket, with an early stop; closures and unreachable targets return the right value (None versus depart); argues why waiting restores the property Dijkstra needs; near-linear complexity; recognises why minute-by-minute simulation and Bellman-Ford do not scale.

clarifications.q: Does a segment's travel time change while I am on it?
clarifications.a: No. It is fixed by the bucket of the minute you enter.

clarifications.q: Which bucket does a car entering exactly on a boundary use?
clarifications.a: The new one. Minute t is in bucket t // bucket_min, so with 15-minute buckets minute 15 is in bucket 1.

clarifications.q: What does None in a profile mean?
clarifications.a: The segment cannot be entered during that bucket. A car that entered earlier still finishes. Only the hardest replays contain closures.

clarifications.q: Can there be two segments between the same two junctions?
clarifications.a: Yes, for example a road and a parallel express lane, with different profiles. Consider each.

clarifications.q: Is waiting free?
clarifications.a: Yes. You only minimise the arrival minute; there is no cost for waiting.

clarifications.q: What if I depart after the last bucket ends?
clarifications.a: The last bucket's travel times apply, for every later minute.

hints: Define leave(t): the earliest minute you can reach the far end of one segment if you are at its start at minute t. Because you may wait, leave(t) never decreases as t grows. Why does that matter?

Entering now gives t + profile[b]. Waiting only helps if you enter at the first minute of a later bucket k, which gives k * bucket_min + profile[k]. Take the minimum, and stop scanning once a bucket starts after the best exit you already have.
With a non-decreasing leave(t) that never returns a time earlier than t, Dijkstra ordered by arrival minute is correct again.
followups: Without waiting, show a two-bucket profile where entering later gets you out sooner. Why does plain Dijkstra fail on it?
A trip planner asks for the latest departure from source that still arrives at target by a deadline. How would you answer it?
A live incident replaces one segment's profile for the next hour. What do you recompute for queries already answered, and what do you keep?
Add turn restrictions and turn costs at junctions. How does your search state change, and what does that do to the graph size?
You serve millions of queries an hour over a continental network. Which precomputation speeds up static shortest paths, and what about time-dependence makes it harder?

rules.ask: How many rounds can your relaxation need on 60 000 junctions, and what does each round cost?
How many minutes does your loop cover for a long trip, multiplied by 180 000 segments? What would you change?
Dijkstra assumes that reaching a junction later never lets you leave earlier. What in your code guarantees that here, and what would break it?
How many later buckets do you scan per segment, and exactly when can you stop scanning?
What admissible estimate would you use when travel times depend on the time of day?

templates.title: Best bitrate plan for a recorded network trace
templates.subtopic: state design over buffer levels, adaptive video streaming

sections.scenario: A video platform's playback team evaluates its adaptive-bitrate logic offline. Each video is encoded at several renditions (a bitrate ladder), and the player picks one rendition per segment as it streams. The team replays recorded network traces and wants a yardstick: the best possible plan for a trace when the whole trace is known in advance, the "offline optimum" commonly used to judge adaptive-bitrate heuristics. Higher quality scores more; stalls (rebuffering) and quality switches cost.
sections.problem: Implement best_plan_score(throughput, ladder, segment_ticks, max_buffer, switch_penalty, stall_penalty). The video has len(throughput) segments of segment_ticks ticks each (1 tick = 100 ms). For every segment choose one rendition from ladder, a list of (kbps, quality). Downloading segment i at a rendition of kbps takes ceil(kbps * segment_ticks / throughput[i]) ticks. The buffer starts at 0 ticks, and segments download one after another: a download of d ticks with b ticks buffered stalls playback for max(0, d - b) ticks, after which the buffer holds min(max(b - d, 0) + segment_ticks, max_buffer) ticks (a full buffer makes the player wait before its next request; that wait costs nothing). The score of a plan is the sum of its qualities, minus switch_penalty times the sum of |quality change| between consecutive segments, minus stall_penalty times the total stall ticks. Return the best score over all plans. {{trace_rule}}
sections.constraints: Up to 200 segments, up to 6 renditions, segment_ticks ≤ max_buffer ≤ 300, throughput ≥ 1 kbps. Integer arithmetic throughout. Trying every plan is len(ladder) ** len(throughput); expect at most O(segments × renditions² × (max_buffer + 1)).
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical ladders, quality scores and traces. The offline optimum ignores throughput prediction on purpose: it is an upper bound to compare real players against, not a player. There is no special case for startup: the buffer starts empty, so the first download is a stall.
sections.criteria: Chooses the state (previous rendition, buffer) and explains why it is sufficient; exact integer ceiling; correct stall, cap and switch-penalty rules including the first segment; complexity bounded by the integer buffer range; distinguishes the offline optimum from an online player; discusses pruning and plan reconstruction.

clarifications.q: Does the first segment's download count as a stall?
clarifications.a: Yes. Startup delay is charged at the same rate as any other stall.

clarifications.q: Is the switch penalty per switch or per quality point?
clarifications.a: Per quality point: going from quality 22 to 44 costs 22 * switch_penalty. The first segment has no switch.

clarifications.q: Does waiting with a full buffer change the next download?
clarifications.a: No. throughput[i] holds for the whole download of segment i, whenever it starts.

clarifications.q: Do I return the plan?
clarifications.a: No, only the best score. Several plans can tie.

clarifications.q: Is quality always increasing with kbps?
clarifications.a: In these ladders, yes, but do not rely on it.

hints: To score the rest of the video you do not need the whole history: the previous rendition and the buffer level are enough.
The buffer is an integer from 0 to max_buffer, so there are at most len(ladder) * (max_buffer + 1) states after each segment. Keep the best score per state.
Integer ceiling: -(-a // b).
followups: Return the plan as well, with a deterministic tie-break. How much extra memory does that need?
With the same previous rendition, is a state with more buffer and a higher score ever worse than one with less of both? How would you use that to prune states?
A two-hour film in 2-second segments at 10 ms resolution with a 60-second cap: what happens to your state space, and how would you coarsen time while bounding the error you introduce?
Production players do not know future throughput. How would you use this optimum to evaluate a new heuristic across thousands of traces, and which numbers would you report?

rules.ask: Show a three-segment trace where taking the best rendition the current throughput allows loses to a lower one.
How many plans are there for 150 segments and 5 renditions?
What is your memo key, how many distinct keys can there be, and how deep does the recursion go for 200 segments?
math.ceil(kbps * segment_ticks / throughput) divides in floating point. When can that differ from an integer ceiling, and how do you avoid the question entirely?
Prove that more buffer never hurts. Which two parts of the buffer formula does the proof rely on?

templates.title: Debug a rebuffering-ratio rollup from player heartbeats
templates.subtopic: deduplication keys, ordering, metric definitions, ratio of totals

sections.scenario: A video player sends heartbeats to a quality-of-experience pipeline. Each heartbeat says how long one viewing session spent in one state (playing, buffering, paused or seeking) during one interval. A daily job rolls them up per video: watch time, join time (the wait before playback starts), rebuffering time and the rebuffering ratio, which dashboards use to compare encodings and delivery networks. Since a player update, watch time is far below the player's own counters, the rebuffering ratio jumps around for videos with few views, and the job has crashed twice. The rollup below is the suspect.
sections.problem:
Fix playback_quality(heartbeats) so that it meets this specification. Each heartbeat is {"session", "video", "seq", "state", "ms"}: during interval seq (1, 2, 3, … within the session) the session spent ms milliseconds in state. {{delivery_rule}}

  1. Retries. A heartbeat whose (session, seq) was already counted is a retry and is ignored. Two intervals of one session with the same state and the same ms are different intervals.
  2. Order. Each session's intervals are read in seq order, whatever order they arrived in.
  3. Classification. playing is watch time. buffering before the session's first playing interval is join time. buffering after it is rebuffering, except buffering that follows a seeking interval before playback resumes (a seek wait), which counts as neither. A seek before the first playing interval changes nothing. paused and seeking count as nothing.
  4. Output. {video: {"sessions", "watch_ms", "join_ms", "rebuffer_ms", "rebuffer_bp"}}. sessions counts distinct sessions, including sessions that never started playing. rebuffer_bp is rebuffer_ms * 10000 // (watch_ms + rebuffer_ms) from the video's totals, and 0 when that denominator is 0.
sections.constraints: Keep the function's name and output format. Up to 200 000 heartbeats; O(n log n) time.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical heartbeat format and numbers, simplified. Definitions of join time and rebuffering differ between players and analytics vendors; this specification fixes one of them for the exercise. A session's heartbeats always name the same video.
sections.criteria: Finds and explains every bug with its symptom; deduplicates on (session, seq); orders by seq within a session; resets the seek wait when playback resumes; computes the ratio from totals and guards the zero denominator; counts abandoned sessions; keeps the fix minimal; adds a test per bug.

clarifications.q: Does a session that never started playing count?
clarifications.a: Yes. It adds one to sessions and its buffering to join_ms, and contributes nothing to the ratio.

clarifications.q: Does a pause end a seek wait?
clarifications.a: No. Only a playing interval ends it.

clarifications.q: Why basis points?
clarifications.a: An integer avoids comparing floats: 125 bp is 1.25 %.

clarifications.q: Is a retry always identical to the original?
clarifications.a: In this exercise, yes. Identify it by (session, seq) all the same.

clarifications.q: How many bugs are there?
clarifications.a: Several, of different kinds. The tests point at each one.

hints: Write down what identifies one interval, then compare it with the key the code deduplicates on. How often does a player send two consecutive 10-second playing heartbeats?
Print one session's heartbeats in the order the job reads them.
Trace after_seek through play, seek, buffer, play, buffer.
One session watched 60 s with a 0.65 s stall, another 4 s with a 3 s stall. Work out the video's ratio from the totals, then see what the code reports.
What happens for a viewer who gave up during startup?
followups: A dashboard compares two delivery networks by rebuffering ratio. Why is "ratio of totals" versus "average of session ratios" a product decision, and when would you show both?
Heartbeats from offline or flaky sessions arrive hours late. How does the daily job handle them, and when is a day's number final?
In a distributed streaming job, where do you deduplicate on (session, seq), and how long do you keep the keys?
A player release changes the heartbeat interval from 10 to 5 seconds. Which metrics must not move, and how would you check that before the release reaches everyone?

rules.ask: What exactly goes into your seen-set, and how much memory does it need for a day of heartbeats?
You sort per session. In a streaming version, what do you do with seq 7 arriving after you already emitted that session?
A 4-second clip with a 3-second stall and a two-hour film with none: what is the video's ratio under each definition, and which would you put on a dashboard?
Where do you guard the division, and what should a video that nobody managed to play show?

templates.title: Click-to-conversion attribution pipeline with late conversions
templates.subtopic: keyed joins, attribution windows, late data, restatement

sections.scenario: An advertising platform reports conversions to advertisers: a purchase or sign-up is credited to the ad click that led to it, if it happens within the advertiser's conversion window (up to {{window}} after the click). There are about {{daily_clicks}} ad clicks a day. Conversions arrive two ways: from a tag on the advertiser's site within seconds, and from advertiser uploads of offline conversions (a sale closed in a CRM, for instance) up to {{upload_lag}} after the conversion. Both carry the click identifier the platform attached to the landing-page URL. Advertisers see conversions by the day of the click, in their account's time zone, within {{freshness}}.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline that joins conversions to clicks and produces the conversion reports. Cover where click state lives and for how long, the join key and the window check, duplicate conversions (a tag that fires twice, an upload that is re-sent), the advertiser's choice to count every conversion or one per click, late and out-of-order data, restating past days as late conversions and click corrections arrive, how outputs stay idempotent, and how you prove the numbers are complete.
sections.constraints: Conversions never change what advertisers are charged for clicks, but a click later found to be invalid (automated traffic, accidental double clicks) is removed from reports and from charges, up to a few days later; its conversions must disappear with it. A report for a past day can change only by restatement, never silently. The click identifier is opaque; the pipeline must not rely on user identities.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, windows and lags are hypothetical. Conversion windows, counting options and offline conversion imports are described in general terms from public advertising documentation; the design is yours. Each conversion carries an advertiser-supplied order id or transaction id when one exists.
sections.criteria: Click store keyed by click id with retention of window plus upload lag; a pending buffer for conversions whose click has not landed, with a deadline and a reason when it expires; conversion deduplication on a business key; every and one-per-click counting derived from the same deduplicated facts; reports by click day in the account time zone; restatement by idempotent partition overwrite with versioning; invalid-click corrections that retract conversions; completeness checks against click and conversion counts; capacity and hot-key awareness.

clarifications.q: Can a conversion arrive before its click is in the click store?
clarifications.a: Yes: the tag can fire within a second of the click, while click logs land in batches.

clarifications.q: Can one conversion match several clicks?
clarifications.a: Not by identifier: a conversion carries one click id. Several conversions can match one click.

clarifications.q: How late can an upload be?
clarifications.a: Usually within {{upload_lag}}; advertisers sometimes re-upload months later. Anything outside the window is rejected with a reason.

clarifications.q: What is the reporting grain?
clarifications.a: Campaign, ad group and conversion action, by the click's day in the account's time zone.

clarifications.q: Who corrects invalid clicks?
clarifications.a: A separate filtering system emits a correction (click id, invalid since) after the fact. You consume it.

hints: With a click identifier on every conversion, the join is a keyed lookup, not a search. What decides how long a click must stay joinable?
Report by click day means a conversion today can change a number from {{window}} ago. Plan for restatement from day one.
Deduplicate conversions on a business key (advertiser, conversion action, order id), falling back to (click id, action, conversion time) when there is no order id.
followups: Size the click state you must keep joinable for {{window}} plus {{upload_lag}}. Where does it live, and what is its access pattern?
A conversion arrives for a click id you have never seen. What do you do with it now, and what do you do in an hour?
A batch of clicks from four days ago is marked invalid. Walk through every table and report that changes, and how advertisers find out.
An advertiser complains their CRM shows 1 240 conversions for last week and the report shows 1 180. How do you investigate?
Advertisers ask for a data-driven attribution model instead of last click. What in your pipeline survives, and what has to change?

rules.ask: Your join keeps state for {{window}}. What is the state size, and what happens when a worker holding it restarts?
An upload arrives {{upload_lag}} late. Is it past your watermark, and what does your pipeline do with it?
What is the read pattern on your click store at peak conversion rate, and how do you keep a hot advertiser from creating a hot key?
The same order id arrives from the tag and from an upload with different values. Which wins, and how do you record it?
How far back can a restatement reach, and how do you keep an advertiser's export from seeing a half-written day?

incidents: An advertiser fixes a bug in their CRM export and re-uploads the last {{upload_lag}} of offline conversions; a tenth of the order ids changed format, so the re-upload looks like new conversions.
One hour of click logs from one region lands six hours late; during that time conversions arrive for click ids the join cannot find.
A daylight-saving change moves the account-time-zone day boundary, and two advertisers' daily totals no longer match their own systems for that day.

templates.title: Search query-log rollup with hot queries and mergeable sketches
templates.subtopic: partitioning, shuffle skew, approximate distinct counts, privacy floors

sections.scenario: A search analytics team publishes a daily dataset for product and research teams: for every country and normalised query, the number of searches, the approximate number of distinct users, the click-through rate on results, and the most common refinements (the next query the same user typed within the same search session). The logs hold about {{daily_queries}} searches a day across {{countries}} countries. A query appears in the dataset only if at least {{min_users}} distinct users searched it, a privacy floor. On the day of a major news event a single query made up {{hot_share}} of all searches; the daily job ran six times longer than usual, one stage spent hours on a handful of tasks, and the dataset missed its deadline of {{deadline}} after midnight.
sections.problem: Design the daily batch pipeline on a distributed SQL or dataflow engine. Cover how the raw logs are laid out, query normalisation, sessionisation for refinements, the aggregation and how it survives a hot query, how you count distinct users approximately and merge counts across partitions and days, how the privacy floor is applied when counts are approximate, late-arriving logs and reruns, the output layout, and what the job costs.
sections.constraints: Raw logs carry a pseudonymous user id that must not appear in the output. The privacy floor is a hard rule: a query below {{min_users}} distinct users must never be published, even by way of a refinement list or a rollup that could be subtracted from another. Logs for a day can arrive up to a few hours after midnight. Downstream teams also want weekly and monthly distinct users per query without rescanning raw logs.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, shares, thresholds and deadlines are hypothetical. Sessions here are a user's searches with gaps of at most 30 minutes; the exact definition is yours to state. Approximate distinct counts such as HyperLogLog are available in public cloud warehouses and dataflow engines.
sections.criteria: Raw logs partitioned by date and clustered sensibly; normalisation versioned; separate shuffles for sessionisation (by user) and aggregation (by country and query) with partial aggregation and skew handling; mergeable distinct-count sketches stored per day and merged for longer periods; a conservative, stated rule for the privacy floor with approximate counts, applied to refinements and rollups too; idempotent partition overwrite for reruns with versioned outputs; bot traffic filtered or capped; cost reasoning in terms of bytes scanned and shuffled.

clarifications.q: How exact must distinct users be?
clarifications.a: Within a few percent for published numbers, except at the privacy floor, where you decide how to be safe.

clarifications.q: Are refinements counted per user or per search?
clarifications.a: Per pair of consecutive queries in a session; publish a refinement only if the pair itself clears the floor.

clarifications.q: What does normalisation include?
clarifications.a: Case folding, whitespace and punctuation, Unicode normalisation; not spelling correction.

clarifications.q: Can the job rerun a day?
clarifications.a: Yes, and it must replace that day's output exactly, never append to it.

clarifications.q: Is the hot query known in advance?
clarifications.a: No. A different query is hot every time.

hints: A group-by on query sends every row of the hot query to one task. Partial aggregation before the shuffle (combiners, two-phase aggregation, salting the key) spreads it.
Distinct counts do not add up, but sketches merge: keep one per (country, query, day) and merge them for weeks and months.
Sessionisation needs every search of one user together, ordered by time; refinements then come from consecutive pairs. That is a different shuffle key from the aggregation.
followups: Walk through the hot query in your plan: which stages see all of its rows, and how many tasks share the work?
A HyperLogLog sketch with about 1.6 % standard error says 103 users for a query; the floor is 100. Do you publish it? What rule would you adopt, and what does it cost in coverage?
Monthly distinct users per query: how do you build it from daily outputs, and what would go wrong if you stored only the daily estimates?
Logs for the last two hours of a day arrive after your job ran. What do you do, and how do downstream readers know the day was restated?
Finance asks why this job's compute cost doubled this quarter. How would you find out, and which design choices would you revisit first?

rules.ask: How many salt buckets do you choose for a query you did not know would be hot, and what does the second aggregation cost?
An exact distinct count per (country, query) needs which shuffle, and how big is it on the hot day?
What precision do you choose, how many bytes per sketch, and how many sketches do you store per day?
Sessionisation shuffles by user. What happens to a user with a million searches a day, and is that user a person?
Your rerun overwrites a day while a weekly job reads it. What does the weekly job see?

incidents: The hot query makes up {{hot_share}} of a day's searches; one aggregation task runs for hours while the rest finish in minutes.
An automated client sends tens of millions of searches under a handful of user ids; the sessionisation stage fails on memory, and those users would dominate refinement pairs.
A change to query normalisation ships mid-month, so the same query appears under two normalised forms in the monthly rollup.

templates.title: Search sessions and query refinements
templates.subtopic: event model, sessionization, nested versus flat facts, data contracts

result_types: web results, ads, image packs and a direct-answer box
web results, ads, a video carousel, a map pack and a direct-answer box

sections.scenario: A web search engine serves about {{daily_searches}} searches a day. Each results page shows a mix of {{result_types}}, and the mix changes as product teams add new result types. Search quality analysts want to study how people search: which queries are refined (rewritten, extended or corrected) and into what, how often a session ends in a click, how often a page ends with no click because the answer was already on the page, and where on the page clicks land. A search session here is a run of one user's searches with no gap longer than {{session_gap}}. Query text is sensitive: in this scenario a query string may appear in any shared table only if at least {{min_users}} distinct users issued it that day.
sections.problem: Design the event model and the analytical model. Define the events the serving and client sides emit (search issued, results page served, results seen, click, back-to-results, query edited) and the contract that governs them. Define the analytical tables: the results page with what it showed and at which positions, the session, and the refinement relationship between consecutive searches. Decide whether a results page is stored as one row with a nested, repeated list of results or as one row per shown result, and say which questions each shape serves. Define "refinement", "click-through" and "answered on the page" precisely enough that two analysts get the same number.
sections.constraints: Clicks and client events arrive minutes to hours after the page was served; some never arrive (the user closed the tab). A page can be served twice for one search (a reload) and must not count twice. The model must absorb a new result type without breaking existing queries. Rare queries never appear as text in shared tables.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, the session gap and the privacy threshold are hypothetical. Users are identified by a pseudonymous key, signed-out users by a short-lived browser key; nothing joins either key to an identity. A results page has a server-assigned page id that the client echoes on every event.
sections.criteria: Clear grains (search/page, shown result, interaction) joined by page id; precise, reproducible definitions of refinement, click-through and answered-on-page, with missing-event handling; sessionization with a stated gap, late-data handling and a close; a reasoned choice between nested and flat shapes; contract versioning and additive evolution for new result types; the privacy threshold enforced at the point of publication, including derived tables; each incident diagnosed with a guardrail.

clarifications.q: Does a spelling correction applied automatically count as a refinement?
clarifications.a: No. A refinement is a new search the user issued; an automatic correction is an attribute of the page that was served.

clarifications.q: Is a click on an ad a click-through?
clarifications.a: Report organic and ad clicks separately and say what the combined metric means; analysts mostly want organic.

clarifications.q: How do I know a result was seen and not just served?
clarifications.a: The client sends a "results seen" event with the positions that entered the viewport. It can be missing.

clarifications.q: Can a session span midnight?
clarifications.a: Yes. Decide which day it belongs to and say why.

clarifications.q: Who consumes these tables?
clarifications.a: Quality analysts with SQL, experiment analysis, and dashboards for the search product teams.

hints: Separate the facts by grain: one row per search (the page served), one row per result shown on it, one row per interaction. The page id joins them.

A refinement is a relationship between two searches in one session. Store it as an edge (previous search → next search, with the kind of edit), derived after sessionization, not as a column on the click.

A nested, repeated "results" field keeps a page and its results together and scans cheaply for page-level questions; a flat result-impression table is easier to aggregate by position and result type. Either can be derived from the other.
followups: Write the precise definition of "answered on the page" you would publish, including how you treat pages whose "results seen" event never arrived.
Sessionization with a {{session_gap}} gap: how do you compute it incrementally when late events keep arriving, and when is yesterday's session table final?
A new result type ships tomorrow. Show the schema change, the contract version, and what an analyst's existing query returns before and after.
Analysts want "the top refinements of query X". How do you serve it when X itself or most of its refinements fall under the {{min_users}}-user threshold?
At {{daily_searches}} searches a day, which table is partitioned and clustered on what, and which question does each choice make cheap?

rules.ask: An analyst wants click-through by position and result type across a month. Walk through the query on your nested table and what it scans.
How many rows a day does that table hold at {{daily_searches}} searches, and what does a page-level question (did this page get any click?) cost on it?
A click for a page arrives three hours late. Does it change any session boundary, and which tables must be rewritten?
Where exactly is the {{min_users}}-user rule enforced, and how do you stop a rare query from leaking through a refinement edge or a join?
The same search is served twice because of a reload, with two page ids. How do you decide it is one search?

incidents: A client release stops sending the "results seen" event on one platform; "answered on the page" jumps for that platform overnight and a product team celebrates a win that is a missing event.

A new result type launched without a contract version bump; the client sends it with position 0, every organic result on those pages shifts by one position, and click-through by position for the top result drops sharply.
A privacy review finds rare query strings in the refinement-edge table: each was common on the day it was issued, but its refinement target was issued by fewer than {{min_users}} users.

templates.title: Recommendation impressions and feedback as training labels
templates.subtopic: point-in-time correctness, delayed labels, deletion propagation

surfaces: the home feed and the up-next list
the home feed, the up-next list and the short-video feed

sections.scenario: A video platform recommends videos on {{surfaces}}, about {{daily_impressions}} recommendation impressions a day. Viewers respond in many ways: they click or ignore, watch for some seconds or to the end, like or dislike, choose "not interested" or "don't recommend this channel", or answer an occasional satisfaction survey. The recommendation team trains models on examples of the form "this video was shown to this viewer in this context; here is what happened", with labels measured over a {{label_horizon}} horizon after the impression. Viewers can delete items from their watch history or pause it, and in this scenario deletions must be honoured in every derived dataset within {{deletion_sla}}.
sections.problem: Design the data model that turns impressions and feedback into training examples. Cover: the impression record (what was shown, where, in which position, by which model version, with which candidate set), the feedback events and how each attaches to the impression that caused it, the label definitions and when a label is final, the features joined to each example as of the moment of the impression (never later), and how a history deletion or pause flows through impressions, labels, features and already-built training sets.
sections.constraints: No feature value may come from after the impression (no leakage). A label is final only after its horizon has passed; a training run must know which labels are final. A watch can start from a surface other than the impression (the viewer searched for the video later); the model must say whether that counts. Training sets must be reproducible, except where a deletion requires a change.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, horizons and the deletion window are hypothetical. Viewers are identified by a pseudonymous key. The product's public controls (watch-history deletion and pause, "not interested", "don't recommend channel") are used in their general public meaning.
sections.criteria: Impression id generated at serving and carried through every event; feedback attached by id with a stated surface rule; labels in their own table with explicit horizons and finality; point-in-time features (logged snapshot or effective-dated join) with leakage named; reproducible training sets with a defined change path for deletions; deletion propagation through raw, derived, features and training sets, including backups; experiment and selection bias named; each incident handled with containment and a guardrail.

clarifications.q: Is an impression a video that was rendered, or one that was on screen?
clarifications.a: Both are logged; you decide which one is a training example and say why.

clarifications.q: How long after an impression can a watch be credited to it?
clarifications.a: Within the {{label_horizon}} horizon, and only when the watch starts from that surface; other watches are a separate signal.

clarifications.q: Can one impression produce several feedback events?
clarifications.a: Yes: a click, a watch of some length, a like, and later a "not interested" on the same video.

clarifications.q: Does "don't recommend this channel" affect old examples?
clarifications.a: It is feedback on the impression where it was given, and a filter on future candidates; it does not rewrite history.

clarifications.q: What does a history deletion remove?
clarifications.a: The watch and everything derived from it: its labels, features computed from it, and the examples that contain it.

hints: Log the impression with a unique id at serving time and carry that id into every client event. Joining feedback by (viewer, video, time window) instead creates double attribution.
Store features as they were served (a feature snapshot logged with the impression) or as effective-dated rows with a point-in-time join; either way, never join "current" features.
Labels are a function of feedback within a window. Materialise them as a separate table keyed by impression id with a final_at time, not as columns on the impression row.
followups: Define the watch-time label precisely: which watch counts, how a rewatch or a partial watch is treated, and the label's value for an impression that was never clicked.
A training run starts at noon. Which impressions can it use, given the {{label_horizon}} horizon, and how does the data model tell it?
A viewer deletes one video from their watch history. Trace the deletion through every table and every training set built in the last {{deletion_sla}}.
The team wants a feature "viewer's watch count for this channel in the last 7 days" for every example. How do you compute it point-in-time correctly at {{daily_impressions}} impressions a day?
Two models serve the same surface in an experiment. How do you keep their examples apart, and what bias appears if you train the next model only on the winner's impressions?

rules.ask: The same video was recommended twice in one hour on two surfaces and watched once. Which impression gets the watch under your join?
The feature table is updated hourly. Show me an example where your join leaks information from after the impression.
A like arrives two days after the impression. Which row changes, and how does a training run that already read it stay reproducible?
The deleted watch is inside a training set that a model was already trained on. What does your design do with the set, and with the model?
Surveys reach a tiny fraction of impressions. How do you store them so they are usable as labels without biasing the rest?

incidents: A training run used impressions from the last hours, before their {{label_horizon}} horizon had passed; recent examples look like non-watches, and the new model quietly learns to under-rank fresh uploads.

A client release drops the impression id from watch events on one surface; a fallback join on viewer and video credits each watch to every impression of that video that day, and watch-time labels for that surface inflate while the other surfaces look unchanged.
An audit finds deleted watches still present in a feature table rebuilt from a backup taken before the deletions, beyond the {{deletion_sla}} commitment.

templates.title: Unique reach and frequency for ad campaigns
templates.subtopic: non-additive measures, mergeable sketches, privacy thresholds

sections.scenario: An advertising platform shows video and display ads, about {{daily_impressions}} impressions a day across {{campaigns}} active campaigns. Advertisers want unique reach (how many distinct people saw the campaign) and frequency (how many saw it once, twice, three or more times) for any date range up to {{max_range_days}} days, by campaign, ad group, country, device type and age bracket, and across a chosen set of campaigns ("how many people did my two campaigns reach together, and how many saw both?"). In this scenario a reach number below {{min_audience}} people is never shown.
sections.problem: Design the data model that serves these numbers. Explain why reach cannot be stored as a daily count and summed, and choose what to store instead: exact per-person aggregates, mergeable cardinality sketches (for example HyperLogLog, which public analytical warehouses expose as aggregate functions that build and merge sketches), or a combination. Define the grain of each stored aggregate, how a date range, a dimension filter and a set of campaigns are answered, how frequency is answered (a cardinality sketch alone cannot), how accuracy is stated to advertisers, and how the privacy threshold is applied to every number, including differences between numbers.
sections.constraints: Arbitrary date ranges must answer in under 2 seconds. Totals in a report must not contradict each other in ways an advertiser notices (reach for two campaigns together never exceeds the sum of their reaches). Late impressions (up to 3 days) and invalid-traffic removals (up to 14 days later) change past days. Person identity is a pseudonymous key per signed-in user or device; cross-device matching is out of scope.
sections.assumptions: Volumes, thresholds and ranges are hypothetical, as is the dimension list. Sketch precision is a parameter you choose; quote its relative error as about 1.04/√m for m registers, as the HyperLogLog literature does.
sections.criteria: States why reach is non-additive before choosing storage; sketch grain and precision chosen with storage and error computed; date ranges, slices and campaign sets answered by merging; frequency solved separately with an honest cost; late data and invalid-traffic removal handled by rebuilding the affected grain; consistency rules on screen (no negative overlaps, union bounded); the threshold applied to published numbers and to differencing attacks; each incident traced to its cause with a guardrail.

clarifications.q: Is an approximate number acceptable?
clarifications.a: Yes for reach, if you state the error and the report stays consistent; billing never uses reach.

clarifications.q: Can an advertiser pick any combination of dimensions?
clarifications.a: Any one or two of the listed dimensions, plus date range and campaign set.

clarifications.q: Do invalid-traffic removals have to change reach?
clarifications.a: Yes. Removed impressions must not count, including in past days already reported.

clarifications.q: Is "people who saw both campaigns" required?
clarifications.a: Yes, as an overlap figure, with the same threshold applied.

clarifications.q: Which frequency buckets?
clarifications.a: 1, 2, 3, 4–5, 6–10 and 11+, for the chosen range.

hints: Distinct counts are not additive across days, campaigns or dimensions. Sketches are mergeable: store one per (day, campaign, dimension slice) and union them at query time.
Intersections by inclusion–exclusion (|A| + |B| − |A ∪ B|) inherit the error of all three estimates; small overlaps can come out negative.

Frequency needs per-person counts over the range. Either keep a per-person, per-campaign, per-day count table and aggregate it for the range, or precompute fixed ranges; say which ranges you can afford exactly.
followups: Choose the sketch precision and compute the storage for one year at your grain. What does doubling precision cost and buy?
Invalid-traffic removal arrives 14 days later for 0.4% of one day's impressions. Which stored objects do you rebuild, and how does an advertiser see the change?

An advertiser compares reach for "country = X" and "country = X and device = mobile" and subtracts them. How can that difference expose fewer than {{min_audience}} people, and what do you do about it?
Serve exact frequency buckets for a custom {{max_range_days}}-day range for a campaign with 300 million impressions. What do you precompute, and what is computed on demand?
Two campaigns' overlap is estimated as negative. What do you show, and how do you keep reach(A ∪ B) ≤ reach(A) + reach(B) on screen?

rules.ask: What precision do you pick, what relative error does it give, and how do you tell an advertiser the number is approximate without confusing them?
Run your exact query for a {{max_range_days}}-day range over {{daily_impressions}} impressions a day. What does it scan and how long does it take?
A person sees the campaign on Monday and Tuesday. How many times does your weekly reach count them?
Both campaigns reach about 40 million people and overlap by 30,000. What is the error on your overlap estimate compared with the overlap itself?
Your threshold hides small cells. Show how an advertiser can recover a hidden cell by subtracting two visible ones, and how you stop it.

incidents: After a precision change in the sketch builder, sketches built before and after cannot be merged; reports whose ranges cross the change date fail, and a hurried fix that casts old sketches mixes precisions silently.

Invalid-traffic removals for one day were applied to the daily impression totals but not to the stored sketches; reach for that day stays above the number of valid impressions for some small ad groups.
A researcher shows that by querying overlapping country and device slices for a campaign whose total reach is just above {{min_audience}}, it is possible to isolate a group of fewer than ten people.

templates.title: Places that merge, close and move — a place-visit model
templates.subtopic: entity identity and merges, SCD type 2, privacy-thresholded aggregates

sections.scenario: A maps product lists about {{places}} places (shops, restaurants, parks, stations), each with a name, category, location, opening hours and status (open, temporarily closed, permanently closed). Listings change constantly: owners edit hours, two duplicate listings are merged into one, a business moves to a new address, a place closes and a different business opens at the same spot. From users who have opted in to location history, the product infers about {{daily_visits}} place visits a day, and it publishes an hourly "how busy is it usually" profile per place, built from the last {{history_weeks}} weeks. In this scenario an hour's profile value is published only when at least {{min_visitors}} distinct visitors contribute to it over the window.
sections.problem: Design the data model. Cover: the place entity and its identity (what a place id means, what happens to ids on a merge, a split or a move), the history of place attributes (which changes are type 2 history and which are corrections), the visit fact (grain, keys, the confidence of the inference, and which place version it refers to), and the busyness aggregate (grain, how it is rebuilt as visits age out of the {{history_weeks}}-week window, and how the privacy threshold is applied). Then show how an analyst answers "visits per week for this café for the last year" when the café was merged with a duplicate listing four months ago.
sections.constraints: A place id given to an external caller must keep working after a merge (it resolves to the surviving place). Visit history must follow a merge but must not follow a closure followed by a new business at the same location. Raw visits are kept for at most {{history_weeks}} weeks; only aggregates live longer. Opening-hours edits must not rewrite which hours visits happened in.
sections.assumptions: Counts, windows and thresholds are hypothetical. Visit inference (from location to a place, with a confidence score) exists upstream and is out of scope; it can be re-run with a better model. Public maps platforms document that a place's id can become obsolete and should be refreshed; that general behaviour is assumed here.
sections.criteria: Surrogate key distinct from external ids, an alias table with merge time, reversible merges and cycle protection; type 2 attribute history with corrections handled distinctly; visits referencing the identity at inference time and resolved through aliases at query time; closure-then-new-business modeled as a new place; a busyness aggregate with a rolling window, incremental rebuild and an honest distinct-visitor count under key rotation; retention of raw visits enforced; each incident traced with a guardrail.

clarifications.q: When two listings merge, which id survives?
clarifications.a: One of them, chosen by the listings team. The other becomes an alias that resolves to it.

clarifications.q: Is a moved business the same place?
clarifications.a: In this scenario yes, if the listing says it moved; a closure followed by a new business is a new place, even at the same address.

clarifications.q: Can a merge be undone?
clarifications.a: Yes, rarely (two listings were wrongly merged). Model it so that it is possible.

clarifications.q: Do visits store coordinates?
clarifications.a: No. A visit stores the place reference, the visit window rounded to the hour, a confidence, and a pseudonymous visitor key that rotates.

clarifications.q: Does a temporarily closed place still get a busyness profile?
clarifications.a: It keeps its history but publishes nothing while closed.

hints: Separate the stable surrogate key from the externally visible ids. An alias (redirect) table maps every id ever issued to the current surviving key, with the time of the merge.
Attribute history (name, category, hours, location) is type 2 on the surrogate key; corrections of wrong data are a different operation from real changes and should be recorded as such.

Store visits against the place as it was identified when the visit was inferred, and resolve to the surviving entity at query time through the alias table, so a merge (or its reversal) never rewrites the visit fact.
followups: Write the query shape for "visits per week for the last year" across a merge, and show what changes if the merge is reversed next week.
A place's category changes from "café" to "bakery". Which reports should see the old value for old visits, and which the new one for all visits?
The visit-inference model is improved and re-run over the last {{history_weeks}} weeks. How do you replace visits and aggregates without a period where both versions are counted?
How do you apply the {{min_visitors}}-visitor threshold when the visitor key rotates, and what does that do to the count of distinct visitors?
At {{places}} places and {{daily_visits}} visits a day, how do you partition the visit fact and keep the busyness rebuild incremental?

rules.ask: The merge turns out to be wrong a week later. How many visit rows does your design rewrite twice, and what did reports show in between?
A typo in a place's name is fixed. Does that create a new version in your history, and what does an analyst see when grouping by name?
A café closes and a gym opens at the same address next month. Show how your model keeps their visit histories apart.
The visitor key rotates daily. How does your threshold count distinct visitors over {{history_weeks}} weeks, and is the count an over- or under-estimate?
Place A was merged into B, then B into C. How does a lookup of A resolve, and how do you prevent a cycle?

incidents: A bulk merge job joined thousands of chain-store listings into one place per brand by name; their visits now resolve to a single place and its busyness profile shows a city-wide crowd.
After a merge reversal, the alias table still sends the restored listing's old id to the other place, so an external integration shows the wrong opening hours for a week.

A place with exactly {{min_visitors}} contributors in most hours published a profile computed with rotated visitor keys counted as distinct people, so the real number of contributors was far below the threshold.

templates.title: Last-click conversion attribution, reported by click date
templates.subtopic: attribution windows, deduplication, counting rules, fan-out

sections.scenario: An advertiser runs search, display and video campaigns. Every ad click is recorded with the campaign and a pseudonymous visitor_key; the advertiser's site records conversions (purchases, sign-ups, quote requests) for the same keys and uploads them, sometimes more than once. Each conversion action has its own attribution window and counting setting in conversion_actions. This extract has the actions {{actions}}. The marketing team wants conversions per campaign reported on the day of the click that earned them, next to that day's clicks, so the cost and the result of a click land on the same day.
sections.problem:
Write one PostgreSQL query that returns click_date, campaign_id, clicks, conversions, conversion_value_micros: one row per UTC date and campaign with at least one click, ordered by click_date, campaign_id. The rules, applied in this order:

  • Duplicates. {{dedup_rule}}
  • Attribution (last click). A conversion is credited to the same visitor's click with click_ts ≤ conv_ts ≤ click_ts + window_days of the conversion's own action (both ends inclusive), choosing the latest such click; when two qualify at the same instant, the higher click_id wins. A conversion with no qualifying click is unattributed and appears nowhere.
  • Counting. {{counting_rule}}
  • Reporting. click_date is the UTC date of the credited click. clicks counts that date's clicks for the campaign; conversions counts the counted conversions credited to them, and conversion_value_micros sums their value_micros (0 when there are none).
sections.constraints: One SQL statement (CTEs allowed). PostgreSQL. The sample has {{clicks}} clicks and {{conversions}} conversion rows; production has billions of clicks a month, so say how your query would scale.
sections.assumptions: Hypothetical schema, campaigns, windows and values; money is in micros (millionths of the currency unit). Clicks and conversions are already joined to visitors by a pseudonymous key; how that key is built is out of scope. Timestamps are UTC.
sections.criteria: Deduplication before attribution with NULL order ids kept apart; an inclusive window per action and clicks only at or before the conversion; last click with a deterministic tie-break; the counting rule applied per click, not per visitor; reporting by click date over a click grid with zero rows kept and no fan-out; deterministic order; can discuss scale and the restatement that late conversions cause.

clarifications.q: Is a conversion exactly window_days after the click still credited?
clarifications.a: Yes. Both ends of the window are inclusive.

clarifications.q: Can a click made after the conversion receive credit?
clarifications.a: No. Only clicks at or before the conversion qualify.

clarifications.q: A visitor clicked two campaigns before converting. Who gets the conversion?
clarifications.a: The latest qualifying click only; this report does not split credit.

clarifications.q: Should a campaign-day with clicks but no conversions appear?
clarifications.a: Yes, with conversions 0 and value 0.

clarifications.q: The conversion happened the day after the click. Which day is it reported on?
clarifications.a: The click's day.

hints: Pick the credited click per conversion with CROSS JOIN LATERAL (… ORDER BY click_ts DESC, click_id DESC LIMIT 1), or with ROW_NUMBER() over the joined candidate pairs.
Deduplicate before attributing, with ROW_NUMBER() over the duplicate key. Check what your partition does to rows whose order_id is NULL.
Aggregate clicks and conversions to (date, campaign) separately, then join: counting clicks after joining conversions multiplies them.
followups: Rewrite the attribution without LATERAL (a range join plus ROW_NUMBER()). Which would you run over billions of clicks, and how would you partition or cluster the tables so the join stays local?
A conversion arrives 25 days after its click, inside a 30-day window. Which already-published click date changes, and how do you tell the marketing team when a day's numbers are final?
Replace last click with a rule that splits credit across all qualifying clicks (for example linearly). What changes in the model and in the query?
The advertiser also wants conversions reported by conversion date. Should that be a second table or a column on the first, and why do the two never sum to the same daily totals?

rules.ask: A conversion lands exactly window_days after its click. Does your condition credit it, and should it?
Two sign-ups have a NULL order_id. What does your partition do with them?
One click has three conversions. How many clicks does your query report for its campaign that day?
Which day is a conversion reported on in your output, and which day should it be?
The visitor clicked campaign A on Monday and campaign B on Tuesday, then bought on Wednesday. Who gets the credit under your query?

incidents: The site's tag fires twice on the confirmation page after a release, and every purchase is uploaded twice with the same order id but timestamps a few seconds apart; reported conversions double for campaigns whose query ignores order ids, and duplicates with a NULL order id cannot be caught at all.

Last week's report by click date was sent on Monday; conversions that arrive during the rest of the attribution window keep raising last week's numbers, and the marketing team asks why the "same report" changes every day.

templates.title: Search performance reports for site owners
templates.subtopic: log joins, fan-out aggregation, privacy thresholds, interactive serving

sections.scenario: A web search engine gives site owners a free performance report. Owners verify a property (a URL prefix such as https://www.example.com/, or a whole domain including every subdomain and protocol) and then see clicks, impressions, click-through rate and average position, filterable and groupable by query, page, country, device and date, for the last {{history_months}} months. About {{properties}} properties are verified, and search results generate around {{daily_impressions}} result impressions per day. In this scenario the reporting rules are: a URL counts an impression when it appears on a results page the searcher saw; a click is a click on that URL's result; average position is the topmost position the property held on each results page, averaged over the pages where it appeared. Queries issued by fewer than {{min_searchers}} distinct searchers in a day are never shown as rows, but their clicks and impressions still count in the chart totals.
sections.problem: Design the pipeline and serving system behind this report: from search serving logs (results pages with the URLs shown and their positions, and click events) to the numbers an owner sees.
