Cover joining clicks to impressions, mapping URLs to properties when properties overlap, the two aggregation modes (by property and by page), the rare-query privacy rule, storage and serving for interactive filtering over {{history_months}} months, data freshness of {{freshness}} for recent days, and how a day is corrected after it was published.
sections.constraints: No searcher identifier, IP address or raw log line ever reaches the reporting store. Interactive reports return in under 2 seconds at p95 for any property, however large. When grouped by property, one results page counts at most one impression for the property even if it shows three of its URLs; when grouped by page, each URL counts. Totals must equal the sum of all rows plus the withheld rare-query rows, and the report must explain why the rows do not add up to the total.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds and retention periods are hypothetical. One URL can belong to several verified properties at once (a domain property and two URL-prefix properties inside it, owned by different teams). Clicks arrive in the logs up to a few hours after the impression.
sections.criteria: Joins clicks to impressions within the log boundary with a defined lateness window; attributes URLs to all matching properties with an efficient prefix lookup; implements property-mode de-duplication per results page correctly and separately from page mode; computes the privacy decision inside the log boundary and ships no identifiers; stores additive sums (impressions, clicks, sum of top positions) so any grouping is correct; lays out storage per property and date with indexes for query filtering; versions published days and restates visibly; handles skewed properties; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the rare-query threshold applied per day or over the date range the owner selects?
clarifications.a: Per query per day in this scenario. Be ready to discuss what changes if it had to hold over any range.

clarifications.q: Do owners need data for the current day?
clarifications.a: A preliminary view within {{freshness}} is wanted, clearly labelled, and replaced by final numbers.

clarifications.q: How many properties can one URL belong to?
clarifications.a: Usually one or two; a few large organisations verify dozens of nested prefixes.

clarifications.q: Can owners export rows?
clarifications.a: Yes, through the report and an API, under the same privacy rule and with a row limit per request.

clarifications.q: What is the largest property?
clarifications.a: A few properties see more than a billion impressions a day across millions of distinct queries.

hints: Join and attribute in the log domain first: one record per (results page, URL, position, clicked) before anything is grouped. Every later aggregate derives from that.
Property mode needs a de-duplication step per results page per property; page mode does not. Decide where that happens so you do not count twice.
The privacy rule needs a distinct-searcher count per query per day, which needs searcher identity — compute it inside the log boundary and ship only the decision.
followups: Walk through how one results page showing two URLs from www.example.com becomes rows for a domain property and a URL-prefix property that both contain those URLs.
Owners filter by a query substring over {{history_months}} months on a property with millions of distinct queries. How is the store laid out so that answers in 2 seconds?
The threshold now has to hold over any date range the owner picks, not per day. What breaks in a precomputed design, and what would you build instead?
A logging defect inflated positions for 2 days of published data. How do you restate those days, and what do owners and the export API see while it happens?
Storage cost is dominated by the long tail of tiny properties. What do you change, and what do those owners lose?

rules.ask: One property gets more than a billion impressions a day across millions of queries. What happens to the worker that owns that key, and how do you split it without breaking the per-property de-duplication?
A URL matches a domain property and three nested prefix properties. How do you find all of them per impression at this volume without a scan of every property?
The privacy decision uses an approximate distinct count near the threshold of {{min_searchers}}. Which way should the error lean, and how do you make it lean that way?
An owner groups by country, then by date. How do you store position so both averages are correct when you combine rows?
Owners pulled the old numbers through the API yesterday. How do they learn the day changed, and what does your store keep about the earlier version?

incidents: A serving change starts logging a results carousel as a single position. For 2 days, average position shifts for about 8% of properties, and owner forums notice before your monitors do.

One news publisher's domain property produces 30% of a day's attributed rows during a breaking story. The daily aggregation for that day runs 9 hours and misses the {{freshness}} target for the preliminary view of every property.
An export bug returns rows for queries below the {{min_searchers}}-searcher threshold for 3 hours before it is caught.
A log storage outage delays one region's click logs by 7 hours; impressions for that region are on time, so click-through rate for the preliminary view drops sharply for that region.

templates.title: Budget pacing for search ad campaigns across regions
templates.subtopic: pacing control, multi-region consistency, billing reconciliation

sections.scenario: An advertising platform runs an auction for every search results page that can show ads: about {{auctions_per_sec}} auctions per second served from {{regions}} regions. Around {{campaigns}} active campaigns each have an average daily budget in the advertiser's own time zone. Advertisers pay per click for most campaigns and per thousand impressions for some. In this scenario the budget rule is: a campaign may spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day, but never more than 30.4 times its average daily budget in a calendar month; any spend above those limits is not charged. Advertisers also expect spend to be spread across the day rather than exhausted at 9 a.m. The auction servers see a spend signal that lags reality by about {{signal_delay}}.
sections.problem: Design the spend tracking and pacing system. Cover how billable events (impressions, clicks) become spend, how each auction server decides whether a campaign may enter an auction and with what pacing, how spend and budget state are shared across {{regions}} regions, how you bound overdelivery given clicks that arrive minutes after the impression and a lagging signal, day and month boundaries in many time zones, invalid-click filtering that later removes charges, and how the advertiser's invoice reconciles with what the pacing system believed.
sections.constraints: The eligibility check sits on the auction path and may add at most a few milliseconds; it cannot call a remote counter per auction. A region must keep serving ads if it loses contact with the others. Charges are never above the stated limits, so overdelivery is the platform's cost, not the advertiser's. Spend shown to the advertiser must be within a few minutes of reality and must reconcile exactly with the invoice at month end.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, delays and budget figures are hypothetical; the budget rule above is the rule for this scenario. Most campaigns have small budgets; a few spend millions a day.
sections.criteria: Distinguishes auction-time, reported and billed spend; local, conservative eligibility with budget shares per region and background rebalancing; accounts for in-flight exposure and signal delay with an explicit overdelivery bound; a pacing controller with a target curve and damping; idempotent spend aggregation keyed by event id; correct day and month boundaries per advertiser time zone; invalid-click credits flowing to billing and pacing; reconciliation from billing to the invoice; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Does the auction need exact remaining budget?
clarifications.a: No. It needs a fast, local, conservative answer; exactness lives in billing.

clarifications.q: How late can a click arrive?
clarifications.a: Most within a minute of the impression; some hours later, and still billable.

clarifications.q: How long until invalid clicks are removed?
clarifications.a: Most within hours by an automated filter; some days later after review. Removed clicks are credited.

clarifications.q: Can an advertiser change the budget mid-day?
clarifications.a: Yes, and it should take effect within a minute.

clarifications.q: Which time zone defines the day?
clarifications.a: The advertiser's account time zone, including days with a daylight-saving change.

hints: Separate three numbers: spend the auction believes (fast, approximate), spend the advertiser sees (minutes), and spend that is billed (exact, final). Each has its own pipeline and owner.
Give each region a share of the remaining budget it can spend locally, and rebalance shares in the background. Think about what happens to a share when its region goes dark.
A click that has not happened yet is still exposure. Estimate in-flight cost from recent impressions.
followups: What exactly does an auction server hold in memory per campaign, how is it refreshed, and what does it do when the data is older than expected?
A campaign with a small budget gets 500 clicks in 10 seconds after a news event. How much can it overspend with your design, and what bounds it?
One region is cut off for 20 minutes. What can it still spend, and what happens to its unused share when it returns?
Invalid-click filtering removes 4% of yesterday's clicks for one campaign, after the day closed. What changes in spend, in pacing and on the invoice?
How would you smooth delivery across the day so a campaign does not exhaust its budget early, and how do you know the controller works?

rules.ask: At {{auctions_per_sec}} auctions per second across {{regions}} regions, what is the round-trip cost of that counter on the auction path, and what happens when it is unreachable?
Your spend stream is {{signal_delay}} behind. How much budget can a high-spend campaign burn in that time, and what compensates for it?
How does your controller react to a traffic spike it has never seen at that hour without oscillating between spending everything and spending nothing?
An advertiser in a time zone with a daylight-saving change has a 23-hour day. What happens to the pacing curve and to the twice-daily-budget limit?
A click event is delivered twice to your spend stream and once to billing. Which number is wrong, and who notices?

incidents: A breaking-news story multiplies query volume tenfold for 30 minutes on a topic where hundreds of small campaigns advertise. Several exceed twice their daily budget before the spend signal, about {{signal_delay}} behind, catches up, and the overdelivery is the platform's cost.

A network partition isolates one of the {{regions}} regions for 20 minutes. It keeps serving on its local budget shares; when it rejoins, two other regions have already reallocated part of those shares.
The invalid-click filter is delayed for 6 hours, then removes 3% of the day's clicks at once. Advertiser dashboards show spend going down, and pacing releases budget for the rest of the day.
A daylight-saving change means one time zone's day has 25 hours. Pacing for every campaign in that zone runs out of budget an hour before its day ends.

templates.title: Playback quality telemetry for a video platform
templates.subtopic: sessionisation, quality-of-experience metrics, high-cardinality alerting

sections.scenario: A video platform serves on-demand and live video to {{concurrent}} concurrent viewers at peak. The player sends an event when playback starts, stalls, resumes, switches quality, errors or ends, and a heartbeat every {{heartbeat_s}} seconds while a session is open. Operations watches quality of experience: time to first frame, rebuffer ratio (stall time divided by stall time plus play time), average bitrate and playback failure rate, sliced by country, network operator (about {{networks}} of them), device class, app version and serving location. A cache cluster or a peering link that degrades must be visible within {{alert_minutes}} minutes; player teams compare adaptive-bitrate algorithms in experiments using daily, exact numbers.
sections.problem: Design the telemetry platform: the event schema, ingestion from clients on unreliable networks, reconstructing each playback session, computing the quality metrics in real time and in a daily batch, detecting regressions across thousands of slices without paging on noise, and serving both the operations dashboards and the experiment analyses.
sections.constraints: Mobile clients lose events and may send them late or twice; sessions often end without an end event (the app is killed). Client clocks are unreliable. Real-time numbers may be approximate if labelled; the daily experiment tables must be reproducible. No viewer identity is needed for quality metrics, and none should be kept in the quality store.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, intervals and slice counts are hypothetical. Live events can triple concurrency within minutes.
sections.criteria: Event schema with cumulative per-session counters and an idempotency key; session reconstruction with a stated timeout and late-event policy; ratio-of-sums metrics stored as additive numerators and denominators; event-time processing with protection against bad client clocks; per-slice baselines, minimum-volume rules and hierarchical localisation for alerting; separate real-time (approximate, labelled) and daily (reproducible) paths; treats "no data" as a signal; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Do heartbeats carry deltas or running totals?
clarifications.a: Your choice. Say why.

clarifications.q: How is a session identified?
clarifications.a: The player generates a playback session id per video start; it is not tied to the viewer's account in this telemetry.

clarifications.q: What counts as a stall?
clarifications.a: Playback stopped waiting for data after it had started. Seeking and the initial load are not stalls.

clarifications.q: How many slices could alert?
clarifications.a: Country × network × device class × serving location gives millions of combinations; most have little traffic.

clarifications.q: What do experiment owners need?
clarifications.a: Per-arm daily metrics with confidence intervals, computed the same way every time.

hints: Make heartbeats carry cumulative counters for the session (play time, stall time, stall count, bytes). Then a lost heartbeat costs freshness, not correctness.
Rebuffer ratio for a slice is total stall time over total watch time — a ratio of sums. Averaging per-session ratios answers a different question.
Alert on slices with enough traffic to be significant, against a baseline for that slice and hour, and roll up the hierarchy to find where the problem actually is.
followups: A session's last heartbeat arrives and then nothing. When do you close it, what do you record, and what happens if an event for it arrives 40 minutes later?
How do you compute rebuffer ratio per slice every minute over {{concurrent}} concurrent sessions, and how do you combine slices into a country view?
A degraded cache cluster affects viewers in two countries on three networks. How does your detection name the cluster instead of paging six times?
An experiment arm shows 4% less rebuffering, but its sessions are 9% shorter. How do you decide whether the new algorithm is better?
An app release changes how stalls are reported. How do you notice that this is a measurement change rather than a quality change?

rules.ask: One session watches 5 seconds with a 1-second stall; another watches an hour with none. What does your metric say about the slice, and what should it say?
A viewer pauses for 20 minutes and resumes. With your gap, is that one session or two, and what does it do to time to first frame?
Client clocks are unreliable. Which timestamp drives your windows, and what do you do with an event whose client time is two days in the future?
A slice with 40 sessions at 3 a.m. crosses your threshold every night. How do you keep paging meaningful across millions of slices?
The constraint says no viewer identity in the quality store. What do you lose without it, and how do you answer a question that seems to need it?

incidents: A live sports final triples concurrency in 10 minutes, from {{concurrent}} toward three times that. Ingestion lag for the quality stream reaches 6 minutes, longer than the {{alert_minutes}}-minute detection target.
An app release starts counting buffering after a seek as a stall. Rebuffer ratio for that app version rises 40% overnight while every other version is flat.
A sampling config meant for 10% of clients ships at 100% for one platform. Event volume from that platform rises tenfold and its slices dominate the dashboards.
One network operator's traffic arrives 2 hours late after an ingest outage in its country; real-time dashboards showed that operator as healthy (no data) during the outage.

templates.title: Live road speeds and ETA accuracy from location probes
templates.subtopic: map matching, privacy aggregation thresholds, offline evaluation

sections.scenario: A maps product estimates live traffic from devices whose users have opted in to share location. Each device sends a location probe every few seconds while navigating or moving: a rotating anonymous identifier, latitude and longitude, accuracy, timestamp, speed and heading. About {{probes_per_sec}} probes arrive per second. The road network has around {{segments}} directed segments. Routing needs a current speed per segment, with no more than {{update_every}} between refreshes, and the ETA team wants to know how accurate the predicted arrival times were — by region, road class, time of day and trip length. In this scenario a segment's live speed may be published only if at least {{min_devices}} distinct devices contributed to it in the window.
sections.problem: Design the system: ingestion, matching noisy probes to road segments, computing live segment speeds with late and bad data, the privacy rules from collection to storage, publishing speeds to routing, and an offline pipeline that measures ETA accuracy by comparing each navigation trip's predicted arrival with the actual arrival.
sections.constraints: Raw probe tracks are kept only briefly (hours) and never joined to an account. Speeds below the {{min_devices}}-device threshold are not published; routing falls back to historical speeds. Routing reads a consistent snapshot: it must never see half of an update. The ETA accuracy pipeline may keep per-trip records longer, but only the fields it needs.
sections.assumptions: All volumes, thresholds and retention periods are hypothetical. Map data updates add, split and retire segments a few times a week.
sections.criteria: Device-keyed, sequence-based map matching followed by a re-key to segments; traversal-based segment speeds with a robust statistic and filtering of non-traffic probes; event-time windows with a lateness policy and clock sanity checks; the distinct-device threshold applied before publishing, with rotation handled; versioned, atomic snapshots tied to a map version; historical fallback and blending; short raw retention with only derived data kept; an ETA accuracy pipeline with clear trip rules and weighting; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Can a probe be matched to a segment from its own position alone?
clarifications.a: Not reliably: GPS error is often wider than the gap between parallel roads. You need the device's recent sequence.

clarifications.q: How long does the rotating identifier last?
clarifications.a: Long enough to follow a short sequence of probes; it rotates, so long tracks cannot be stitched together.

clarifications.q: Which probes should not count toward traffic speed?
clarifications.a: Ones that do not represent traffic: a parked car, a pedestrian on the pavement, a bus in its own lane. You decide how to detect them.

clarifications.q: What is "actual arrival" for ETA accuracy?
clarifications.a: When the navigation session ends at the destination. Trips that are abandoned or rerouted to a new destination need a rule.

clarifications.q: How fresh must ETA accuracy reporting be?
clarifications.a: Daily is fine.

hints: Map matching is stateful per device: partition by the rotating identifier and match short sequences, not single points.
Aggregate per segment per window from matched traversals (entry time, exit time, length), not from instantaneous speeds, and use a robust statistic.
Publish speeds as a versioned snapshot with the map version it was computed against; a segment id means nothing without the map version.
followups: How do you shard map matching and segment aggregation, given that they are keyed by different things?
A downtown segment at rush hour has 400 devices; a rural road at 3 a.m. has one. What does routing get for each, and how do you blend live and historical speeds?
A map update splits a highway segment into three in the middle of the day. What happens to live speeds, the threshold count and the historical baseline?
How do you measure ETA accuracy so that the result is not dominated by short city trips, and what do you do with trips where the driver ignored the route?
Someone asks to keep raw tracks for 90 days to improve map matching. What do you answer, and what would you offer instead?

rules.ask: Map matching needs each device's sequence of probes. If you key the stream by segment, how does one worker see a device's path across segment boundaries?
A delivery van stops on the segment for 4 minutes while traffic flows. What does your average say, and what statistic would you use instead?
A grid cell holds a highway and the frontage road beside it. How does a cell-based approach tell their speeds apart?
The identifier rotates. How do you count distinct devices per segment per window without counting one device twice when its identifier changes mid-window?
Raw tracks must be deleted within hours. Which derived data do you keep, and how would you show an auditor nothing longer-lived can be joined back into a track?

incidents: A stadium lets out 60,000 people at once. Probe volume in that city rises to 15 times its usual share of the {{probes_per_sec}} total, most of it from pedestrians walking beside a road whose live speed drops to walking pace.
A map update retires and replaces 2 million segment ids at noon. For 40 minutes the live snapshot mixes old and new ids, and routing falls back to historical speeds across large areas.
A client release on one operating system reports probe timestamps in local time instead of UTC. Probes from those devices land hours away from their real windows.
Overnight, most rural segments fall below the {{min_devices}}-device threshold. A road closure on one of them is invisible to live traffic, and ETAs through it are wrong by an hour.

templates.title: A multi-tenant serverless analytical SQL service
templates.subtopic: storage and compute separation, shuffle, skew, fair scheduling

sections.scenario: A public cloud offers a serverless analytical SQL service: customers load data into tables and run SQL without managing servers. About {{tenants}} customer projects use it, with up to {{concurrent_queries}} queries running at once; the largest tables hold {{largest_table}}. Customers choose between paying per byte scanned (an on-demand pool shared by everyone) and buying reserved compute capacity, measured in units of parallel compute (call them slots). Reserved capacity covers about {{reserved_share}} of the fleet. Tables can be partitioned by date and clustered by up to a few columns.
sections.problem: Design the query service: how storage and compute are separated, how a SQL query becomes a distributed plan of stages, how intermediate data moves between stages (the shuffle), how you schedule work across tenants so reservations are honoured and idle capacity is not wasted, how you handle data skew, how a query survives the loss of workers mid-flight, and how scanned bytes are metered for billing.
sections.constraints: A reserved customer always gets at least its reserved slots within seconds of asking. One tenant's very large query must not starve the on-demand pool for others. Queries are billed by bytes scanned after partition and column pruning, so metering must be exact and repeatable. A worker failure must not fail a query that has run for an hour.
sections.assumptions: All sizes, counts and shares are hypothetical. Storage is columnar, compressed and replicated in a distributed file system; compute nodes hold no durable state.
sections.criteria: Columnar storage with partition and column pruning before any compute; plans as stages connected by a shuffle that is decoupled from workers; broadcast versus shuffle joins chosen on measured sizes, with adaptive replanning; skew detection and key splitting; two-level fair scheduling with guaranteed reservations, lending and preemption of borrowed slots; task-level retries from persisted shuffle data; metering defined on pruned logical bytes once per query, independent of retries; quotas and cost guardrails; adapts to each incident with diagnosis, recovery and prevention.

clarifications.q: Is the service single-region?
clarifications.a: Each dataset lives in one region or multi-region location; queries run where the data is.

clarifications.q: How are joins between a large and a small table handled?
clarifications.a: Your call; say when you broadcast and when you shuffle.

clarifications.q: Can idle reserved capacity be used by others?
clarifications.a: In this scenario, idle slots in a reservation can be lent to other reservations of the same customer first, then to the shared pool, and are reclaimed when needed.

clarifications.q: What does a customer see while a query runs?
clarifications.a: Stage-by-stage progress, bytes processed, slot time used, and the slowest tasks in each stage.

clarifications.q: Are results cached?
clarifications.a: Yes, for identical queries over unchanged tables; a cached result scans and bills nothing.

hints: A shuffle tier that holds intermediate data outside the compute workers lets you add, remove or lose workers between and during stages without restarting the query.
Fair scheduling has two levels: across reservations and the shared pool, then across queries and tasks within each.
Skew is a property of the data, not the plan. Detect it from statistics or runtime sizes and split the heavy keys.
followups: Trace SELECT country, COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) FROM events WHERE event_date BETWEEN … GROUP BY country through your system: which stages, what is shuffled, and on which key.
A join on customer_id has one key holding 30% of the rows. What does your engine do, at plan time and at run time?
A worker dies in the middle of a stage that has run for 40 minutes. What is lost, what is recomputed, and how do you avoid billing the bytes twice?
A reserved customer's dashboard refreshes 200 queries every minute and their reservation is full; queries queue. What do you show them, and what are their options?
How would you meter bytes scanned so that partition pruning, clustering, caching and retries all bill correctly, and how would you prove it to a customer who disputes an invoice?

rules.ask: The "small" table is 40 GB after a customer's filter changes. When does your planner notice, and what happens to the workers already running?
One key holds 30% of the rows. What does the task that receives it do, and how do you split it without breaking the join?
A reserved customer and an on-demand customer both submit at the same time while the shared pool is busy. Who runs first under your queue, and does that honour the reservation?
Spilling keeps the query alive but slows it by 10×. Where does the spill go, and how does the customer find out it happened?
A retried task re-reads its input partitions. How does metering avoid charging the customer twice for those bytes?

incidents: A customer's dashboard runs an unpartitioned scan of a table of {{largest_table}} every minute after someone removes the date filter. Their on-demand bill for the day is 300 times normal, and the shared pool's queue time rises for everyone.
A join on a skewed key leaves one task holding 40% of a stage's input; the query has run for 6 hours with every other task finished.
A rack of shuffle-tier nodes is lost during peak. Several thousand running queries have intermediate data on those nodes.

At month end, reserved customers, whose reservations cover about {{reserved_share}} of the fleet and usually sit partly idle, reclaim their idle slots at once; on-demand queries that were borrowing those slots slow to a crawl.

templates.title: Conversions double-counted, and automated bidding acted on them
templates.subtopic: data correctness with automated downstream consumers

cause: a deduplication step that was skipped after a pipeline migration
a tag change that sent each conversion through two ingestion paths
a backfill that re-imported conversions the stream had already counted

sections.scenario: Your team owns the pipeline that turns advertisers' conversion events (purchases, sign-ups) into the conversion counts shown in advertising reports and consumed by automated bidding, which raises bids for ads that appear to convert well. For {{days}} days, {{cause}} inflated conversions by about {{inflation}} for roughly {{advertisers}} advertisers. Automated bidding responded by bidding higher, so those advertisers spent more than they otherwise would have. An advertiser's analyst noticed that reported conversions no longer match their own sales system. You are the most senior engineer on the pipeline.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would lead the response: the first hour, the first day and the following weeks. Cover stopping the inflation, correcting the data, the effect on bidding and spend, who decides about remediation for advertisers, communication, and prevention. Then tell me about a real incident where wrong data drove automated decisions or customer cost (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: Corrected conversions will change the inputs of bidding models that have already adapted to the inflated numbers. Reports are read through an API by thousands of advertisers' own systems. Remediation for spend is decided with account, finance and policy teams, not by engineering alone.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Contains the pipeline (disable the faulty path, restore deduplication) and the decision effect (exclude the window from bidding with the bidding team); quantifies duplicates with a measured error rate before restating; restates through versioned data with an API signal; coordinates remediation decisions with account, finance and policy owners and supplies an evidence-based spend estimate; factual, timely communication; prevention with invariant monitors (conversions per click, duplicate-key rates) that page an owner; real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Is the inflation still happening when you are told?
clarifications.a: You do not know yet; the first signal is one advertiser's ticket and a rising conversions-per-click ratio on an internal dashboard nobody pages on.

clarifications.q: Can bidding be told to ignore a window of data?
clarifications.a: The bidding team has a mechanism to exclude a date range from learning for affected advertisers; it has costs of its own.

clarifications.q: Do we know exactly which conversions are duplicates?
clarifications.a: Partly. Some duplicates share an order id; some conversion types have no order id at all.

clarifications.q: Who talks to advertisers?
clarifications.a: Account and support teams, with the facts your team provides.

hints: Two things are wrong at once: the reports and the decisions made from them. Contain both.
Measure how well you can identify duplicates before you restate anything; "remove all duplicates" is a claim you need to back with a sample.
Think about the order of operations: correcting conversions while bidding is still learning from them changes its behaviour again.
followups: Your correction removes 20% more conversions than the advertiser tickets suggest. Do you restate all of them? Who decides?
Bidding has already raised bids for {{days}} days. If you restate the data today, what happens to bids tomorrow, and how would you make that transition safe?
Finance asks for an estimate of the extra spend caused. How would you produce it, and how confident would you be?
What signal, threshold and owner would have caught this within an hour?
In your real example, what did you personally decide, and what would you do differently?

rules.ask: The bad data has already been read by bidding and by advertisers' systems through the API. What does a rollback of the pipeline fix, and what does it not?
Some conversion types have no order id. How do you decide what to remove there, and what is your error rate?
That is not your team's decision alone. Who decides, and what evidence do they need from you?
Name one prevention item that actually shipped, and how you know it works.
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: Halfway through a migration that is not paying off
templates.subtopic: course correction, sunk cost, owning your own call

sections.scenario: A year ago you proposed moving the daily batch pipelines that produce watch-time and revenue-share inputs for video creators' analytics from an ageing in-house batch cluster to a newer distributed processing engine. Your proposal promised a 30% cost saving and earlier delivery. Today {{done}} of the jobs have moved. On the new engine those jobs cost {{cost_ratio}} as much as they did before, and {{missed}} of them now regularly miss their morning deadline. The old cluster's hardware lease ends in {{lease}}. The team is tired and mostly wants to push through; your manager has started asking when the savings will show.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would decide what to do now: carry on, pause, roll some jobs back, or change the plan. Cover what you would measure before deciding, the options you would put on the table, who decides, how you tell people that the plan you championed is not working as promised, and how you look after the team. Then tell me about a real time you changed course on a technical decision you had argued for (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: Creators' analytics and payment inputs must stay correct and on time. The lease can be extended once, at a premium, for at most a few months. The team has other commitments this half.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Gathers evidence (per-job cost and runtime, causes, risk to creators) before deciding; frames options from today rather than defending the sunk cost; considers a mixed plan (fix the dominant jobs, pause or roll back the worst, use the one lease extension deliberately); takes the revised plan to the decision owner with an honest account of what was wrong in the original estimate; protects correctness and deadlines for creators; looks after a tired team; improves future estimation (pilots on the hardest jobs first, exit criteria); real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Do you know why the new jobs cost more?
clarifications.a: Not fully. Some jobs were ported line by line; some shuffle far more data than before; nobody has profiled them all.

clarifications.q: Are the missed deadlines visible to creators?
clarifications.a: Not yet. Analytics have been a few hours late on some days; payments inputs have been on time.

clarifications.q: Who approved the migration?
clarifications.a: Your director, on your proposal and estimates.

clarifications.q: Can the remaining jobs stay on the old cluster indefinitely?
clarifications.a: No. The lease ends; extending it once is possible but costly.

hints: Separate the sunk cost from the decision: compare the options from today, with today's numbers.
Find out whether the cost is inherent to the new engine or comes from how the jobs were ported; a few jobs usually dominate.
Telling people early, with data and a revised plan, protects your credibility more than a late success story.
followups: Profiling shows three jobs account for most of the extra cost. What do you do with them, and what with the rest?
Your director asks whether the original estimate was wrong or the execution was. How do you answer?
The team wants to finish the migration before fixing anything. How do you decide whether they are right?
What would you put in place so the next migration proposal is estimated better?
In your real example, what did changing course cost you, and what did you learn?

rules.ask: The lease ends in {{lease}}. Where do rolled-back jobs run after that, and what does a second migration cost the team?
What evidence would make you stop, and when will you have it?
Who does that work, and what does the team stop doing to make room for it?
What assumption in your original estimate failed, and how would you have tested it before committing?
What did you personally decide or do?

templates.title: A reach-estimate accuracy promised before it was measured
templates.subtopic: resetting an external commitment, honesty with evidence

sections.scenario: Your team builds the data behind a campaign-planning tool that estimates how many unique people an advertising campaign will reach for a given budget, audience and schedule. Before your team was consulted, sales leadership told {{pilots}} pilot advertisers that estimates would be accurate {{promised}}, with launch in {{launch}}. Your backtests on past campaigns show a median absolute percentage error of {{measured}}, worse for small audiences and new ad formats. Some pilot advertisers plan to commit budgets based on the estimates.
sections.problem: Tell me what you do: how you make sure your own numbers are right, how and to whom you raise the gap, what you propose instead of the promise, how you work with sales leadership who made it, and how you would stop this from recurring. Then tell me about a real time someone else made a commitment your work could not meet and you had to reset it (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: You cannot move the launch date or change what was said to advertisers on your own. Reach is measured on de-duplicated people with privacy thresholds; you cannot show advertisers individual-level data to explain an error. Improving accuracy substantially would take longer than {{launch}}.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Verifies the error rigorously and by segment before raising it; raises it early, first with the people who made the promise and the product owner, in writing with evidence; brings a constructive alternative (scoped launch for segments that meet the bar, ranges or confidence labels, a clear statement of what the tool is for); helps sales correct the commitment with advertisers; considers advertisers who already acted on estimates; proposes a process so accuracy is measured before it is promised; real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: How was the backtest done?
clarifications.a: Estimates for past campaigns, made with only the data available before each campaign started, compared with the measured reach afterwards.

clarifications.q: Who made the promise?
clarifications.a: A sales vice-president, based on a slide from an earlier prototype.

clarifications.q: Is any part of the product accurate enough?
clarifications.a: Large audiences on established formats are close to the promise; the long tail is not.

clarifications.q: Who owns the product decision?
clarifications.a: A product manager, who reports into a different organisation from sales.

hints: Check your backtest before you challenge anyone: what is the error by segment, and could your measurement be the problem?
Bring a proposal, not just a problem: what can honestly be promised, for which campaigns, and how it is shown to advertisers.
Make it easy for sales leadership to correct course without losing face with advertisers.
followups: The sales vice-president says "just launch; the estimates will improve with data". What do you say?
How would you present uncertainty to advertisers so it is honest and still useful for planning?
One large pilot advertiser has already committed budget based on an early estimate that now looks too high. What should happen?
What process change would make sure a data product's accuracy is measured before it is promised?
In your real example, how did you reset the commitment, and what happened to the relationship?

rules.ask: Advertisers plan with one number. How do you show a range they will actually use, and what do you do for segments where the range is too wide to be useful?
What did you do before going above the person who made the promise, and how did you tell them you were going to?
That takes longer than {{launch}}. What ships at launch in the meantime?
How do you know the backtest is representative of the campaigns pilot advertisers will plan?
What did you personally do or say, and to whom?

templates.title: A design disagreement with a senior peer
templates.subtopic: design review, influence, disagree and commit

proposal: move map matching onto devices so only matched segment traversals are uploaded
replace the streaming live-speed pipeline with a micro-batch job that runs every minute
serve live speeds from one global database instead of per-region snapshots
peer: a principal engineer on the routing team
the staff engineer who designed the current pipeline

sections.scenario: A design review in {{days}} days will decide the next architecture for the live road-speed system of a maps product. The design up for approval, written by {{peer}}, proposes to {{proposal}}. The author is more senior than you, widely respected, and most of your own team likes the design. You have read it closely and believe it has a serious weakness that the document does not examine (for example in failure handling, privacy, cost or freshness), but you are not certain, and you were not asked to review it.
sections.problem: Tell me what you do between now and the review, at the review, and afterwards — whether the design changes or is approved as written. Cover how you test your concern, how you raise it and with whom, what you do if the decision goes against you, and what you do if you turn out to be wrong. Then tell me about a real time you disagreed with a more senior engineer about a design (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: The review date is fixed. You have no formal role in approving the design. Other teams are waiting on the decision.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Engages the author first, privately and with curiosity; makes the concern specific and testable, and tests it proportionately; raises it in the review with evidence and alternatives, not opinions; is open to being wrong and says so when they are; commits fully if overruled while recording the risk and a trigger to revisit; handles a later incident without blame; real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Have you talked to the author?
clarifications.a: Not yet.

clarifications.q: Can you build a prototype?
clarifications.a: A small one, in the time available, if you set aside other work.

clarifications.q: Who approves the design?
clarifications.a: A review group of senior engineers; the author presents.

hints: Talk to the author first and privately; you may be missing context, and they deserve the chance to answer before a group does.
Turn the concern into something testable: a failure scenario, a cost estimate, a measurement.
Decide in advance what you will do if the group decides against you.
followups: The author listens politely and changes nothing. What next?
Your prototype shows the problem is real but smaller than you thought. How do you present that?
The review approves the design as written. How do you behave over the next six months?
A year later, the weakness you raised causes an incident. What do you do and say?
In your real example, what did you change in how you disagree?

rules.ask: What exactly would you say in the first two minutes of that conversation?
The prototype takes a week away from your committed work. Who do you tell, and how do you decide it is worth it?
What would make escalating the right step here rather than raising it in the review?
What does committing look like in practice if you still think the design is wrong?
How do you raise the incident without making it about who was right?

templates.title: A live traffic pipeline that pages every night
templates.subtopic: on-call health, reliability versus feature work

roadmap: expanding live speeds to two new countries
a new incident-detection feature for road closures
migrating to a new map version format

sections.scenario: Your team of {{team}} engineers owns the streaming pipeline that computes live road speeds for a maps product. On-call receives about {{pages}} pages a week, many at night, and only about {{actionable}} of them need any action. Two engineers have said they are thinking of leaving; on-call handoffs are tense. Product has committed the team to {{roadmap}} this half. You have just become the technical lead.
sections.problem: Tell me how you would turn this around: what you look at first, how you decide what to fix, how you negotiate time with product, how you change alerting and on-call practice, and how you will know it worked. Then tell me about a real time you improved an on-call rotation or a system's operational load (STAR, with measurable outcomes), or say that you have not and reason through how you would.
sections.constraints: The roadmap commitment was made before you arrived. You cannot hire this half. Live speeds feed routing for millions of trips, so real failures must still page.
sections.assumptions: The situation and figures are hypothetical.
sections.criteria: Starts with data (page classification over weeks) and with the people (on-call load, attrition risk); defines user-facing objectives and moves alerting to them; removes or downgrades non-actionable alerts with evidence; negotiates a concrete trade-off with product backed by numbers; fixes top causes and automates safe remediation; sustainable on-call practice (handoffs, follow-up ownership, load measured); defines success metrics up front; real example with measurable evidence and personal contribution, or honestly marked as hypothetical.

clarifications.q: Are there service-level objectives?
clarifications.a: Informally: "speeds should be fresh". Nothing written.

clarifications.q: What do the pages say?
clarifications.a: Mostly consumer lag thresholds, a few job restarts, and a weekly batch of "data looks odd" alerts nobody owns.

clarifications.q: Does your manager support pausing features?
clarifications.a: Your manager will support a well-argued proposal with numbers.

hints: Classify a few weeks of pages: actionable or not, cause, time of day, who resolved it and how.
Write the objective that matters to routing (freshness and coverage of live speeds) and alert on burning it, not on internal symptoms.
Bring product a trade-off with numbers: what the roadmap costs if reliability work is not done.
followups: What would your first two weeks look like, concretely?
Product says the roadmap date cannot move. What do you propose?
Which alerts would you delete, and how do you convince the team it is safe?
Six months later, how would you show leadership that it worked?
In your real example, what did you personally change, and what was the measured result?

rules.ask: Which objective would you write for live speeds, how would you measure it from routing's point of view, and what happens when the budget is spent?
One of the alerts you removed would have caught an outage last year. How did you check before removing it?
You cannot hire this half. What do you do with the people you have?
Which page did you automate first, and what did you do to make sure automation could not make an outage worse?
What did you personally decide or do?
